title: Λύκος καὶ αἴξ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 220. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Λύκος θεασάμενος αἶγα ἐπί τινος κρημνώδους ἄντρου νεμομένην, ἐπειδὴ οὐκ ἠδύνατο αὐτῆς ἐφικέσθαι, κατωτέρω παρῄνει αὐτῇ καταβῆναι, μὴ καὶ πέσῃ λαθοῦσα, λέγων ὡς ἀμείνων ὁ παρ’ αὐτῷ λειμών ἐστι, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἡ πόα σφόδρα εὐανθής.
sentences.tr: Lykos theasamenos aiga epi tinos krēmnōdous antrou nemomenēn, epeidē ouk ēdynato autēs ephikesthai, katōterō parēinei autēi katabēnai, mē kai pesēi lathousa, legōn hōs ameinōn ho par’ autōi leimōn esti, epei kai hē poa sphodra euanthēs.
sentences.l: A wolf, having caught sight of a goat grazing upon a certain sheer cave, since he was not able to reach her, kept urging her to come down lower, lest she also fall unawares, saying that the meadow beside him was better, since the grass too was exceedingly full of bloom.
sentences.i: A wolf saw a goat grazing above a sheer cave, and since he could not get at her, he kept urging her to come down lower, in case she should fall before she knew it, saying that the meadow on his own side was better, and the grass there very full of flower.
sentences.n: ἐφικνέομαι takes the genitive of what one reaches. μή with the aorist subjunctive after a verb of urging expresses the thing feared: for fear that she fall. λαθοῦσα is the λανθάνω idiom again, the participle taking the weight in English — 'fall without noticing'. εὐανθής is 'in full bloom', of pasture at its best. Every word of the wolf's concern is pretext.

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ἀπεκρίνατο πρὸς αὐτόν· « Ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐμὲ ἐπὶ νομὴν καλεῖς, αὐτὸς δὲ τροφῆς ἀπορεῖς. »
sentences.tr: Hē de apekrinato pros auton· « All’ ouk eme epi nomēn kaleis, autos de trophēs aporeis. »
sentences.l: And she answered him: « But it is not me you are calling to pasture; it is you yourself who are short of food. »
sentences.n: The emphatic ἐμέ, not the enclitic με, stands first in its clause and carries the whole point: it is not her feeding he has in mind. ἀπορέω takes the genitive of what one is short of. πρὸς αὐτόν after ἀπεκρίνατο is the ordinary Greek fullness where English says simply 'answered him'.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ κακοῦργοι, ὅταν παρὰ τοῖς εἰδόσι πονηρεύωνται, ἀνόνητοι τῶν τεχνασμάτων γίνονται.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai tōn anthrōpōn hoi kakourgoi, hotan para tois eidosi ponēreuōntai, anonētoi tōn technasmatōn ginontai.
sentences.l: So too, among men, the evildoers, whenever they work their wickedness among those who know, become without profit from their contrivances.
sentences.i: So too the evildoers among men: whenever they practise their wickedness on people who know them, they get nothing out of their contrivances.
sentences.n: ὅταν with the subjunctive is the indefinite 'whenever', of what happens as a rule rather than once. ἀνόνητος takes the genitive of the thing one gets no good of. τοῖς εἰδόσι is the participle of οἶδα, a perfect with present sense: those who know, and so are not taken in. τέχνασμα is a contrivance worked up by skill.
